profile.name: electric boogaloo
profile.tagline: A fluid, leg-oriented funk dance combining popping and Oakland boogaloo.
profile.insight: Invented in the mid-1970s and shaped by the group Electric Boogaloos, the style turns human joints into the mechanical parts of a Rubik's Cube.
profile.profile: Electric boogaloo is a street dance style developed around 1975 in California and New York, combining modern popping techniques with earlier Oakland boogaloo forms. Danced to funk music, it is characterized by fluid, leg-oriented movements, rolls of the hips, knees, legs, and head, and the illusion of waves flowing through the body. It became the signature style of the mid-1970s dance group, the Electric Boogaloos.
profile.profile_long:
Electric boogaloo, sometimes referred to on the East Coast of the United States as electric boogie, is a street dance style that emerged around 1975, developing independently in New York and in Fresno, California. It forms a core part of the old school hip-hop dance tradition and is closely related to the earlier Boogaloo street dance performed in Oakland, as well as to popping. While observers occasionally mistake it entirely for the robot, robot imitation is merely a component of the wider discipline.

The style is characterized as a fluid, leg-oriented form danced to funk music, utilizing continuous rolls of the hips, knees, legs, and head. These movements are frequently combined with popping and the visual illusion of waves flowing seamlessly through the body. Over time, practitioners developed a specific lexicon of foundational steps. Among them is the 'Creepin', an entry and exit movement inspired by the cartoon character Goofy, featuring extended legs and arms, sometimes paired with a pointing hand gesture to challenge an opponent. Another key movement is 'Crazy legs', a footwalk invented by Poppin Pete after watching a dancer named Crazy Legs. 

The technical vocabulary also includes 'The Slot'—such as the Fresno—created by John Murphy in Oakland's boogaloo generation. This side-to-side movement ends in a hard pose or 'hit' with the arm and leg on the active side, mimicking a pinball machine slot to keep dancers locked in rhythm. Other foundational techniques include 'Neck-o-flex', the 'Old man' style created by Boogaloo Sam after observing a pedestrian on the street, and the 'Twist-o-flex', where a dancer creates the impression of unnatural, disjointed movement reminiscent of a Rubik's Cube or a modeling clay figure. These innovations cemented electric boogaloo as the signature style of the mid-1970s group, the Electric Boogaloos, who popularized both the dance and its related popping techniques.

sections.origins_and_history: Developed around 1975 in Fresno, California, and independently in New York, electric boogaloo emerged as part of the old school hip-hop dance tradition and funk street dance. It is closely related to the earlier Boogaloo street dance performed in Oakland and to popping, eventually becoming the signature style of the mid-1970s dance group the Electric Boogaloos.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Characterized as a fluid, leg-oriented style utilizing rolls of the hips, knees, legs, and head, combined with popping and the illusion of waves flowing through the body. Key foundational steps include Creepin, Crazy legs, The Slot (such as the Fresno), Neck-o-flex, Old man, Twist-o-flex, and Walk-out.

signature_moves.name: Creepin
signature_moves.description: A foundational step of Boogaloo done in Oakland inspired by cartoon's Goofy, typically done as an entry and exit step with arms out, legs extended.

signature_moves.name: Crazy legs
signature_moves.description: A footwalk created by Poppin Pete by watching a boy called Crazy Legs.

signature_moves.name: Fresno / The Slot
signature_moves.description: A side-to-side movement ending in a hard pose or hit with the leg and arm of the side moved to.

signature_moves.name: Twist-o-flex
signature_moves.description: A technique creating the impression of unnatural body joints by moving and twisting parts in sequence.
